page: Microsoft Azure D64alds_v7 is a compute-optimized virtual machine powered by an AMD EPYC 9V45 processor built on the x86_64 architecture. Running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor, this instance provides 64 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 32 physical cores with multithreading enabled. The CPU operates at a high clock speed of 4.5 GHz and features a cache hierarchy including 1.0 MB L2 cache and 32 MB L3 cache. It supports advanced vector and cryptographic instruction sets, including AVX-512, AVX_VNNI, AES, and SHA_NI.

This server is configured with 128.0 GB of system memory, yielding a low memory-to-core ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. It includes 3780 GB of local storage and is premium storage capable, making it suitable for workloads requiring high-speed local disk access. No GPU accelerators are included in this configuration, and it does not bundle complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data highlights top-tier performance in single-core CPU execution, gzip compression, and PassMark CPU and database operations. Multi-core performance, memory bandwidth reaching 205.53 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads, and Redis SET operations fall into the strong top 25% tier. Large-model LLM inference with 70B parameters drops to average performance, though smaller model inference achieves top-tier text generation speeds.

Given its high-frequency dedicated cores and substantial local storage, the D64alds_v7 offers strong resource density for compute-heavy and storage-reliant tasks. However, the low memory-to-vCPU ratio represents a tradeoff for memory-intensive applications. It is highly suited for high-throughput web serving, database operations, software compilation, and localized data processing tasks where raw CPU speed and local disk capacity are prioritized over massive RAM footprints.

With a low memory-to-core ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU, this server represents a high-compute, storage-capable configuration. It is best suited for high-throughput web serving, database workloads, and compute-heavy tasks that benefit from fast local disk access rather than massive memory allocations.
